Advise scope choice against the five-scope model and its leakage caveats
Build per-team failure handling (admin-disabled OAuth, app transfers)

approval.trigger: None described: the Dev Center OAuth documentation describes no review, approval, listing, directory, or verification step for OAuth clients. Registration is self-serve and users can authorize immediately. (Heroku's add-on program is a separate mechanism and is not how OAuth API access works.)

blockers.detail: Heroku administrators can turn OFF third-party OAuth access to team-owned resources in the team's Settings tab; API calls against team apps then fail. Transferring an app to a team with third-party OAuth disabled can break previously configured services. Your integration can be switched off per customer team, permanently, by someone else's admin.
blockers.howToClear: Detect the failure mode, surface it clearly to the customer, and give their admin the exact setting to change.
blockers.title: Team admins can disable third-party OAuth entirely

blockers.detail: Only five scopes exist: global, identity, read/write, read-protected/write-protected. There are no per-app or per-resource scopes: you request account-wide or team-wide access or nothing, and consent screens say so.
blockers.howToClear: Request the narrowest of the five that works and disclose the breadth honestly to users.
blockers.title: Five scopes, all account-wide

tested: Read-only verification: client registration routes, the web authorization flow, the five-scope model, token lifetimes, and team controls were checked against the current Heroku Dev Center OAuth article (last updated September 29, 2026; no client registered, nothing submitted)
unverified: Whether any review, vetting, or public listing exists for OAuth clients outside the OAuth article (nothing in it mentions one).
The full client-registration field list beyond name and callback URL.
OAuth-client-specific rate limits (the Platform API reference is a separate page, not read for this guide).
An internal inconsistency: the article's refresh example shows expires_in 7199 (~2 hours) while the prose states access tokens expire after 8 hours; the docs do not reconcile this.

alternatives: Direct authorization (a user exchanges their own API token for a long-lived token for their own scripts; not a third-party consent flow)
Team authorization (the same web flow, but a team admin selects a team to own the resulting token; scoped to team resources and cannot perform user-only actions)
flavor.recommended: An OAuth client registered with Heroku (Dashboard, CLI, or Platform API) using the web application authorization flow
flavor.why: This is the third-party flow: the user is redirected to id.heroku.com/oauth/authorize, consents, and your app exchanges the code at id.heroku.com/oauth/token for tokens against the Heroku Platform API. Dashboard registration is documented as the easiest route.

humanMust: Register the OAuth client and custody the client secret
Choose among the five scopes (a breadth decision with real consequences)
Customer team admins control whether third-party OAuth is allowed on their teams at all
name: Heroku
nuances: 'Read' is leakier than it looks: the docs warn that even with read or read-protected, some read-only resources include write credentials in metadata, e.g. log drain definitions often contain embedded basic-auth usernames/passwords or API tokens visible to any integration with read access.
read-protected/write-protected differ from read/write by including runtime secrets such as database connection strings.
Refresh tokens don't expire, but every token exchange or refresh requires the client secret. Tokens are 65 characters prefixed HRKU-, which aids leak detection.
Regenerating or revoking a team token invalidates the current token immediately and permanently.
MFA is mandatory on Heroku accounts, which is why direct authorization exchanges an existing API token rather than a username/password.
prerequisites: A callback URL and an app name (the name is shown to users on the authorization prompt)

steps.detail: Dashboard (easiest), CLI oauth commands, or the Platform API: provide a name (shown on the authorization prompt) and a callback URL; receive a client ID and secret. Store the secret.
steps.title: Register the OAuth client

steps.detail: GET id.heroku.com/oauth/authorize with client_id, response_type=code (the only supported grant type), scope (space-delimited), and state (an anti-forgery token).
steps.title: Redirect the user to authorize

steps.detail: POST to id.heroku.com/oauth/token with grant_type=authorization_code, the code, and the client secret. The response includes access_token, expires_in (web-flow access tokens expire 8 hours after issue), refresh_token (does not expire), token_type Bearer, and user_id.
steps.title: Exchange the code

steps.detail: Call api.heroku.com with Authorization: Bearer <token>. Refresh via POST /oauth/token with grant_type=refresh_token, the refresh token, and the client secret. Revoke with DELETE api.heroku.com/oauth/authorizations/{authorization-id}, which blocks associated tokens from further requests.
steps.title: Call the Platform API; refresh and revoke

tagline: Self-serve OAuth with no review and refresh tokens that never expire, balanced by the coarsest scope model in this library: five scopes, all account-wide, and even 'read' can surface credentials hiding in metadata.

time.active: ~5 min of registration + under an hour of standard flow code
time.total: Same day; no waiting component exists
